# Resolution Adaptation

Also called: Adaptive Resolution, Dynamic Resolution, View-Dependent Resolution

## Overview
Resolution Adaptation is a family of [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) techniques in volume rendering that dynamically adjust the spatial discretization of the rendering process to balance computational cost and visual fidelity. It solves the problem of fixed-cost rendering by varying the resolution of the volume data, the sampling density, or the output framebuffer based on performance metrics (frame time) or visual error metrics. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Adaptive Sampling and Resolution](1412-adaptive-sampling-and-resolution.md) by focusing specifically on the *spatial* or *structural* granularity of the representation (voxel grid, octree nodes, or screen pixels) rather than just the number of samples per ray, and from [Two-stage NeRF Rendering](925-two-stage-nerf-rendering.md) by often operating on the data structure or viewport scale rather than a distinct coarse-to-fine neural [inference pipeline](#5924-inference-pipeline.md).

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of decoupling the rendering resolution from a static global constant. The general loop involves:
1.  **Metric Evaluation:** Computing a scalar value that drives adaptation. This is either a **Performance Metric** (e.g., $t_{actual}$ vs $t_{target}$) or a **Visual Error Metric** (e.g., texel density, gradient magnitude, or structural similarity).
2.  **Discretization Adjustment:** Modifying a resolution parameter $R$. This parameter can represent:
    *   Voxel grid dimensions $(res_x, res_y, res_z)$.
    *   Viewport reduction factor $n \in (0.0, 1.0]$.
    *   Octree node depth or active cut size.
    *   Channel-specific resolution levels $l_i$.
3.  **Rendering:** Executing the volume integral using the adjusted discretization.
4.  **Stability Control:** Applying hysteresis, smoothing, or clamping to prevent oscillation between resolution levels.

Mathematically, the adaptation often follows a proportional control law:
$$ R_{new} = R_{old} + \alpha \cdot (t_{target} - t_{actual}) $$
or a threshold-based step function:
$$ R_{new} = \begin{cases} R_{max} & \text{if } \text{Error} < \epsilon_{min} \\ R_{min} & \text{if } \text{Error} > \epsilon_{max} \\ R_{old} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$

## Subtopics

### [Level-of-detail (LOD) methods](1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md)
[Level-of-detail (LOD) methods](#1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md) maintain responsive frame rates by generating reduced-resolution approximations of the original data during viewpoint [interaction](#41-interaction.md). They solve the problem of computational intensity in volume rendering by dynamically adjusting the discretization (step size, sample count, or spatial resolution) based on a metric of visual error or performance. Unlike static hierarchical structures, these methods adapt in real-time to user manipulation, trading accuracy for speed to ensure interactivity.

### [Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update](2539-dynamic-volume-resolution-alpha-mask-update.md)
This method dynamically adjusts the voxel grid resolution and the active spatial bounding box (AABB) of a volume representation during training to balance computational cost and geometric fidelity. It solves the problem of inefficiently training dense [neural volumes](#912-neural-volumes.md) by pruning empty space via an alpha mask and upscaling the grid only when necessary. It differs from static resolution methods by coupling spatial culling (alpha mask) with discrete resolution upscaling steps, and from continuous adaptive sampling methods by modifying the underlying domain discretization rather than just the ray sampling density.

### [Dynamic Resolution Adaptation](2683-dynamic-resolution-adaptation.md)
[Dynamic Resolution Adaptation](#2683-dynamic-resolution-adaptation.md) is a performance-based acceleration technique that dynamically adjusts the render viewport reduction factor based on previous frame render time and allocated time budget to maintain a target frame rate. It solves the problem of performance instability in volume rendering, where small parametric changes (e.g., transfer function modifications) can cause frame rate dips leading to cybersickness. It sets itself apart from static resolution schemes by continuously shifting the "anchor points" between resolution levels based on the gradient of recent frame times, rather than using fixed blending factors.

### [Mixed-Resolution Multi-Volume Rendering](3193-mixed-resolution-multi-volume-rendering.md)
[Mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering](#3193-mixed-resolution-multi-volume-rendering.md) is a technique where different channels of a multi-volume dataset are rendered at different spatial resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation costs. It addresses the inefficiency of rendering all channels at the highest resolution when some channels have lower frequency content or lower visual importance.

### [Volume Level-of-Detail (LOD) Rendering](4614-volume-level-of-detail-lod-rendering.md)
[Volume Level-of-Detail (LOD) Rendering](#4614-volume-level-of-detail-lod-rendering.md) is a method that maximizes image quality within user-specified frame rate and system constraints (RAM, texture memory, bandwidth) by adaptively modifying the set of rendered cells in an octree. It differs from sibling methods like [Level-of-detail (LOD) methods](1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md) by explicitly maintaining an "active cut" of octree nodes to ensure space is covered exactly once, and by integrating data loading from disk/RAM into the adaptation loop. It builds on [Resolution Adaptation](3063-resolution-adaptation.md) by using error metrics to drive the structural changes in the volume representation rather than just step size or viewport scaling.

### [Focus and Context Multiresolution Rendering](8163-focus-and-context-multiresolution-rendering.md)
[Focus and Context Multiresolution Rendering](#8163-focus-and-context-multiresolution-rendering.md) is a technique to balance processing capacity between a high-detail focus region and a lower-detail context region to improve interactivity in time-critical applications. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Level-of-detail (LOD) methods](1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md) by explicitly separating the scene into two distinct rendering passes with different resolutions and rendering models, rather than adjusting a single global resolution or using [hierarchical data structures](#4133-hierarchical-data-structures.md). The goal is not seamless integration but a tradeoff between quality and speed.

### [Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB)](8219-multiresolution-atlas-buffer-mab.md)
The [Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB)](#8219-multiresolution-atlas-buffer-mab.md) is an acceleration wrapper for [Direct Volume Rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) (DVR) in Virtual Reality (VR) that reduces ray density adaptively based on peripheral vision and Head-Mounted Display (HMD) lens distortion, then reconstructs the full-resolution image via [compositing](#2436-compositing.md). It differs from sibling methods like [Level-of-detail (LOD) methods](1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md) by operating as a post-process/compositing bracket around existing raycasters rather than modifying the volume data structure or traversal logic itself, and unlike [Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update](2539-dynamic-volume-resolution-alpha-mask-update.md) which adjusts voxel grid resolution, MAB maintains the original ray traversal but subsamples the output framebuffer.

#### Mixed Resolution Scene Rendering
Combines full-resolution scene elements with low-resolution high-density volume data by rendering the volume to off-screen targets and projecting them onto a quad [S1]. Setup involves two off-screen cameras (one per eye) and two low-resolution render targets (e.g., 200x200) [S1]. Each frame, the low-resolution targets are drawn for each eye (containing volume data and expensive shaders), the scene is drawn normally at full resolution (meshes, UI), and a quad is drawn in front of the user to project the low-res renders onto it [S1].

#### Resolution and Frame Splitting
High-end systems reduce resolution to 1/2x1/2 [S2, unofficial]. Mid/Low-end systems use frame splitting (similar to RDR2), simplified for clouds not intersecting other objects [S2, unofficial].

## Background
Resolution adaptation in volume rendering originated from the need to handle large datasets interactively. Early LOD methods for unstructured grids and voxel data focused on reducing polygon counts or slice counts [S2, unofficial][S3]. With the advent of [GPU-based raycasting](#6058-volume-raycasting-on-gpu.md) and neural volume representations (NeRFs), dynamic resolution became critical for managing training costs and inference latency [S1][S2, unofficial]. In Virtual Reality, where frame rates are critical to prevent cybersickness, dynamic viewport scaling and peripheral vision-based resolution adaptation (MAB) became standard practices [S1].
